description:
Where a satellite is now, or at a given time: the point on Earth straight below it, its altitude, whether it is sunlit, and its page url. For every satellite in the sky right now use find_satellites_up_now; for when it passes over use find_passes; for its orbit and TLE use get_satellite.

With a place (lat and lon, or location) it also gives where the satellite is in that place's sky (azimuth, apparent elevation, range and whether it is above the horizon), and the place sets the time zone for local times and for reading a time with no offset; without one, times are UTC.

With durationMinutes it also gives the ground track from that time on, one point every stepSeconds (up to a day, at most 720 points of about 0.3 KB each), with the sky fields too when a place is given. lonDeg jumps between 180 and -180 at the antimeridian, so split a drawn line there.

With a list of up to 10 satellites ("where are the ISS and Tiangong now?") it gives where each is at that one moment: positions has one entry per satellite with its name, noradId, url and the fields above (one that can't be found or worked out gets an error there; the others still answer), and time, resolvedLocation and interpretedAs stay at the top. Duplicates are listed once. A ground track takes one satellite, not a list.

A time more than 30 days from the orbital elements' epoch is refused. Read-only, free, no key needed; up to 120 requests per 60 seconds per IP address. A bad input or a failure comes back as an error result (isError) whose text names the problem and what to change. A place name is looked up with OpenStreetMap (one lookup a second, cached), which can add a few seconds; lat and lon or a grid square need none. With more than one satellite it is a heavy call: one at a time per caller; another waits up to 20 seconds, then is refused as busy.

durationMinutes.description: how long a ground track to return, in minutes from time, up to 1440 (a day); about 93 is one ISS orbit. Omit for one position.

lat.description: observer latitude in decimal degrees, north positive (-90 to 90). Give it with lon, or give location instead.

location.description: where the observer is, when lat and lon are not given (they win when both are): a Maidenhead grid square (EN52, EN52ve, EN52ve12), coordinates in any common form ("41.88, -87.63", "41.88N 87.63W", "41°52'48"N 87°37'48"W", a Google Maps link or geo: URI), read locally, or a place name (city, address, landmark) looked up with OpenStreetMap. Optional here: with it, the result adds azimuth and elevation from there.

lon.description: observer longitude in decimal degrees, east positive and west negative (-180 to 180).

satellite.description: NORAD catalog number (as a number or a string) or a name, e.g. 25544, "25544" or "iss"; or a list of up to 10, e.g. [25544, 48274], for where each is at the same moment (no ground track with a list).

stepSeconds.description: seconds between track points, 10 to 3600. Default 60, or wider when needed to keep the track to 720 points; a step you give that would make more is refused, naming the smallest that fits.

time.description: when (with durationMinutes, where the track starts). Default: now. ISO 8601 with Z or an offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00:00-06:00"; a time with no offset, e.g. "2026-11-14T21:00", is read in the observer's time zone, and the result echoes how it was read (interpretedAs). A local time the clocks skip at a daylight-saving change is moved forward, with a note.
